author: Randall W. Forsyth
title: Look Beyond the FANGs
text:
Photo: Bloomberg News By Randall W. Forsyth July 27, 2018 12:56 p.m. ET Poof! David Copperfield, meet Mark Zuckerberg. Instead of making a jetliner disappear on a Las Vegas stage, the chief executive of Facebook made $119 billion evaporate from the social-media giant’s stock-market value on Thursday after uttering some less-than-encouraging words about future growth and expenses.
Our colleagues at Dow Jones Data Strategy observed that not only was this the biggest drop in market cap ever, but it was larger than the market values of 457 of the S&P 500 companies. Yet the ripple through the overall stock market was relatively small, as Wilshire Associates estimated U.S. equities lost only $75 billion that day. And Facebook’s (ticker: FB) drop only brought the shares back to where they were last May, and still above the levels they reached in early Spring after the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
By Friday the damage seemed more widespread, especially in the Nasdaq. The tech-heavy index slumped 1.5%, leaving it down 1.1% for the week. The S&P 500 did manage to end the week in the plus column by 0.6% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average benefited from its lack of new tech to add 1.6% for the week.
Markets took less of a cue from macro factors. The as-expected strong second-quarter gross-domestic-product report showing 4.1% inflation-adjusted annual growth had scant impact, as markets saw through some of the special factors, notably a surge in soybean exports to beat Chinese tariffs imposed in retaliation for U.S. tariffs. While the June quarter was the strongest in 10 years, that performance was enhanced by fiscal stimulus and still-accommodative monetary policy with short-term interest rates at or below inflation, depending on which inflation gauge you use.
To temper the effect of tariffs on farmers, the administration also offered $12 billion in agricultural aid, ahead of November’s midterm elections. That move was anticipated here almost four months ago when the trade tit-for tat began (see “Tariff Talk Isn’t the Only Problem for Stocks,” April 6).
The coming week, however, may be quite different. The calendar is chock-full of important events that the markets have to get past before the August holidays begin in earnest. In addition to the continuing parade of earnings reports, with Apple (AAPL) the biggest name on tap, there’s a heavy slate of economic data and events. Key among those events will be the Federal Open Market Committee meeting, which will wind up on Wednesday, and the monthly employment report for July, due on Friday morning. There is virtually no expectation the Fed’s policy-setting panel will raise its key federal-funds target rate range, from the current 1.75% to 2% range. Once again, it will be a matter of “watch what they say,” since the panel is unlikely to do anything.
What investors, analysts, and economists will be looking for will be clues about future confabs. The futures market puts the probability of a quarter-point rate hike at the Sept. 25-26 meeting at 93%, according to Bloomberg, which is as close to certainty as “damn it” is to swearing. The futures market puts the chance of a hike in December at 70%. None of those odds were altered by the ballyhooed GDP report.
The jobs report could have more impact, however. Expectations are for numbers to follow the recent trend, with a 190,000 increase in nonfarm payrolls plus a downtick in the headline jobless rate of 0.1 percentage point from June’s 4%. More keenly anticipated will be the change in average hourly earnings; a 0.3% monthly rise and a 2.7% year-over-year increase are anticipated. Recall that a surge in hourly pay helped set off the early February correction as it stirred fears of a more aggressive Fed tightening.
Keep an eye on Chinese policy, which Bank of America Merrill Lynch’s strategy team led by Michael Hartnett sees reacting to a “recessionary trend in world trade activity.” In the past three months, there has been monetary easing with two cuts in required reserve ratios and a 7% devaluation of the renminbi or yuan, plus 1.1 trillion yuan ($161 billion) in tax cuts and $1.35 trillion in local bond issuance.
Their suggested trade to take advantage of these moves: go long BRICs (the out-of-favor emerging markets of Brazil, Russia, India, and China) and short FANG (Facebook, Amazon.com [AMZN], Netflix [NFLX], and Alphabet [GOOGL]). Meanwhile, watch the South Korea Kospi for confirmation that Beijing’s moves are working, given the former’s status in the “food chain for China.” The Kospi also tends to move in sync with the Nasdaq, not surprising given the technology emphasis of the Seoul market.
Sounds like you should stay close to market even if you’re heading to beach in August.
What the Weakening Housing Market Means it may not quite rank with Sam Zell’s sale of his office real estate investment trust at the top of the market in 2007, but the end of Chip and Joanna Gaines’ popular HGTV series, Fixer Upper, this year seems almost as propitiously timed.
It isn’t how they planned it, but the final episodes of the popular home-renovation series aired last spring just as the residential housing market began to lose momentum.
Sales of new and existing homes plus starts of new construction all have slumped in recent months, surprising most economists and bulls on residential real estate, including Barron’s, which featured housing in a cover story a few months ago ( “The Housing Market’s Rebound Is Far From Over,” March 3). Since then, however, housing—a major engine of economic growth—has sputtered.
Previously, a shortfall of supply of new and previously occupied homes had been the main culprit holding back sales. Now, it’s also a lack of demand, despite a low unemployment rate of 4% and mortgage interest rates that are low by historical standards.
To paraphrase a gadfly political candidate in New York a few years back, the problem is that prices are too damned high. Home prices remain out of the reach of many , especially first-time purchasers who remain the key initial link of the housing food chain.
“Higher home prices weaken affordability, and first-time home buyers are particularly impacted because prices have increased most for the lower-priced homes they would typically buy,” according to Freddie Mac, the government-sponsored enterprise that provides a big portion of financing to the mortgage market.
Higher borrowing costs are the usual suspect for a slowdown in housing activity. The standard 30-year fixed-rate loan rate last week was 4.54%, up from 3.92% a year ago and 3.41% at the record low in mid-2016. Compared with mortgages with rates twice that high in the not-so-distant past, today’s home loans still seem like bargains.
Indeed, these historically low rates may be inhibiting the trade-up market. Homeowners who took advantage of the low interest rates engineered by the Federal Reserve may find it too expensive to move up even if they can sell at a profit. Downsizing may not save much either, after transaction and moving costs. Then there’s the new tax law that caps the deduction of state and local taxes at $10,000, which covers a fraction of property taxes of expensive houses in high-cost states in the Northeast or in California.
Newsletter Sign-up The good news, ironically, is that these costs may help loosen up the supply of existing homes. Capital Economics points to the high number of vacant houses that are “held off-market for personal reasons.” With interest rates so low, the cost of holding on to empty houses in the hopes of future capital gains has been small.
Meanwhile, existing-home sales dropped for the third straight month in June, falling 0.6%, down 2.2% from a year earlier and dropping at a 6.4% annual rate so far in 2018, notes David Rosenberg, chief economist and strategist at Gluskin Sheff. While tight supplies are a factor, year-over-year price gains of 5.2% are curbing demand along with higher mortgage rates. As a result, home-buying conditions are back to the recession levels of December 2008. Thirty-seven percent of respondents in the latest University of Michigan consumer-sentiment survey—a metric that rarely gets this high—think it’s a bad time to buy because house prices and mortgage rates are too steep.
New houses, not existing ones, are what’s counted in GDP. But Evercore ISI’s Stan Shipley points out that new-home sales fell a steep 5.3% in June after being revised lower in May, while median new-home prices were back down to levels last seen in February 2017. “The housing data over the past two months suggest real residential investment may be only a modest boost to the overall economy in [the second half] of 2018,” he writes in a research note.
As usual, the stock market has sussed out these trends. The iShares U.S. Home Construction exchange-traded fund (ITB) and the SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF (XHB) are down 13% and 12%, respectively, for the year through Thursday. The latter, notwithstanding its name, is dominated by makers of stuff for the home rather than builders. Last week, two of them took a hit after earnings disappointments. Mohawk Industries (MHK), the flooring maker that’s the top holding of the SPDR ETF, fell over 17% after a miss on earnings and a lowered forecast, bringing its year-to-date decline to 35%. Whirlpool (WHR) plunged over 14% after its earnings were hit by higher metal costs caused by increased tariffs.
While residential construction directly accounts for a relatively small portion of GDP, its large multiplier effects have an outsize impact on overall economic growth, Rosenberg points out. Moving into a previously owned home typically results in purchases of new flooring, appliances, and furniture. Brokers’ commissions also figure into the GDP accounting, and could be down with slower sales in the second quarter, according to RDQ Economics.
All of which adds up to a slowdown in housing more than a fresh correction, according to Capital Economics. But that means a shift from a tailwind to a headwind, especially as the Fed continues to move rates up from rock bottom to merely low levels. Well played, Chip and Joanna.
